name: Tinosorb M (bisoctrizole)
lead: Bisoctrizole, sold by BASF as Tinosorb M and listed on ingredient labels as methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol (MBBT), is an ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens and daily-wear skincare in Europe, Asia and other regions. It helps people look better by limiting UV exposure, the main driver of sunburn, tanning, dark spots, wrinkles and other visible photoaging, so users can stay outdoors without the skin damage that shows up on the face over the years.

Chemically it is a phenolic benzotriazole, a white powder that dissolves poorly in both oil and water and is therefore supplied as a roughly 50 percent suspension of microfine particles in the water phase, stabilized with the surfactant decyl glucoside. Descriptions call it a hybrid filter because it absorbs UVA and UVB and is also reported to scatter light [3][1].

Published literature on it includes a controlled trial of a sunscreen containing it for polymorphic light eruption, ex vivo skin studies, contact-allergy reports and photopatch-testing recommendations, and environmental monitoring. Several dermatology reports attribute allergic reactions to Tinosorb M to decyl glucoside rather than the filter itself [4][5][6].
infobox: Permitted in cosmetic sunscreens, up to 10 percent [1]
Not in the OTC sunscreen monograph [7]

paras: Bisoctrizole is a bis-benzotriazole with a methylene bridge, a white powder insoluble in water and poorly soluble in oils. The commercial product is a water-based dispersion of micronised particles stabilised with decyl glucoside; Wikipedia gives the filter's formula as C41H50N6O2 [1][3]. Both the Grokipedia and Wikipedia pages carry sourcing caveats, so these details are provisional.

It is sometimes called a hybrid filter: its benzotriazole structure absorbs UV and dissipates the energy as heat, and the particles are described as also reflecting or scattering some radiation [1][3]. Wikipedia reports that it shows very little photodegradation and is used to help stabilise other filters, but flags these statements as lacking citations [3].

Tinosorb M is typically used alongside other modern filters such as Tinosorb S (bemotrizinol). A 2025 review of US sunscreen regulation lists bisoctrizole with bemotrizinol, drometrizole trisiloxane and TDSA among filters used internationally that offer broad and stable UV protection but are not available in the United States; the authors note a newer FDA over-the-counter monograph order request process may offer a pathway to approve them [7].
The Grokipedia summary reports it is permitted in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan and has not been cleared by the US FDA [1].
A 2003 study evaluated an organo-mineral broad-spectrum sunblock on two ex vivo skin models, using markers of UVB damage (sunburn cells, p53) and UVA damage (vimentin) to assess photoprotection [4].

A 2008 controlled trial in 12 patients with a history of polymorphic light eruption tested a sunscreen containing Tinosorb M, Tinosorb S and butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane under standardised UVA and UVB photoprovocation, with placebo on one side of the body, to assess prevention of the eruption [8].

A 2007 case report described allergic contact dermatitis from the filter [5]. Later reports concluded that decyl glucoside, an alkyl glucoside surfactant in the dispersion, was the cause, and a 2013 report called Tinosorb M containing decyl glucoside a frequent cause of allergic contact dermatitis in the study population [2][9]. A 2017 review of alkyl glucosides describes decyl glucoside as a hidden allergen in Tinosorb M and notes that sensitization rates have been rising in North American data [6].

A European photopatch-testing taskforce recommended that patch testing with decyl glucoside accompany MBBT photopatch tests to separate the reactions [10]. A 2011 case report described positive patch and photopatch reactions to MBBT in patients with atopic and chronic actinic dermatitis [11]. A separate study concluded true photoallergy to sunscreens is rare [12].
A 2018 study measured organic UV stabilisers and filters in sediment of the North and Baltic Seas as part of a hazard assessment [13].

Human research consists of a 2008 controlled study of a combination sunscreen in polymorphic light eruption [8], dermatology case reports and series on contact allergy [5][2][9][11], and a photopatch-testing consensus [10]. No trials of Tinosorb M alone for cosmetic appearance outcomes have been published.

card.summary: A hybrid organic/particulate UV filter in European and Asian sunscreens; reported contact allergies have been traced to a surfactant in its dispersion.
card.note: Not in the US OTC monograph per the cited source.

quick.overview:
Tinosorb M is a broad-spectrum UV filter supplied as fine particles. It is described as working through both absorption and scattering, and it appears in sunscreens sold in the EU and other regions.

The published literature is mostly allergy reports and lab or ex vivo work. No trials were found testing it alone on appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Its benzotriazole structure absorbs UV and dissipates the energy as heat; particles are also said to scatter some light.
quick.risks: Dermatology reports describe allergic contact dermatitis, attributed in several cases to decyl glucoside in the dispersion. A 2010 study found true photoallergy to sunscreens to be rare.

chain: Filter particles absorb and scatter UVA and UVB
Less UV reaches skin cells and collagen
Fewer burns, less tanning and pigmentation
Skin keeps a smoother, more even look over time
angle.text: Applied in a sunscreen, Tinosorb M contributes UV protection across the UVB and UVA range. People who use broad-spectrum sunscreens daily do so to prevent sunburn and the accumulated pigmentation and wrinkling that appear on the face.
